title: Output of the `knowledge.status` MCP tool
description:
The whole response, and the record of what this tool promises about a project's withheld half.

Six required keys, always all six, and a seventh — `integrity` — that appears only when a bounded damage check fired (#30) and is absent, asserting nothing, otherwise. The split that matters among the six is the one the measurement below makes. Four are identical between two projects differing only in an item the caller may not read — `projectId`, `itemCount`, `itemsByStatus`, `schemaVersion` — and two are not: `stateHash` and `appliedMigrations`, which identify the canonical state the counts were read from.

**The counts carry nothing about withheld content, not even a total.** `itemsByStatus` is computed over the surfaceable statuses alone and `itemCount` is the sum of that breakdown rather than the size of the store, so a project whose items are all retired answers `{}` and `0` — the counts a project holding nothing would give (SEC-13, T-17). The counts, and not the whole response: the next paragraph says which two fields still move. This is the claim `knowledge.get` makes in prose when it refuses to distinguish a withheld id from an absent one; a count that included the retired items would answer the same question with a number, and without the caller having to guess an id at all.

**`stateHash` moves for any change to canonical state; `appliedMigrations` moves when a migration is added — and both move for a migration that creates only withheld items.** An edit to an existing migration moves the hash and not the count, so the two are not interchangeable. That both move for an added migration is measured, not conceded in the abstract: two projects built identically except for one extra migration creating a `rejected` item return the same `itemCount`, `itemsByStatus`, `projectId` and `schemaVersion`, and a different `stateHash` and `appliedMigrations` (Milestone 5, review round 8). So T-17's equality — one query against two corpora — holds for this tool's counts and not for its whole response, the way it does for `knowledge.search` and `knowledge.get`.

Both fields stay, and this file is where that decision is recorded rather than in a comment ([#19](https://github.com/theurian/theurian/issues/19)). The justification is per field below, and it is the same shape in both cases: neither carries a bit about *what* was withheld, and this tool takes one argument, so nothing about a request reaches either of them and there is no probe to vary — no extraction oracle, which is the property that made `snapshotId` publishable and `withheldSuperseded` not. A schema cannot enforce that relation between two responses; a validator sees one document. Read the paragraph above as a claim the project owes a differential test, and the constraints below as what this file does hold: which keys exist, and that no retired status may appear among them.

projectId.description: Echoed from the request. Always a registered id: an unregistered one is an error naming the ids that are registered, never an empty status (ADR-0002, SEC-13). Required on every call — there is no process-global current project, because with many agents sharing one daemon an implicit default reports one agent's project to another.

stateHash.description:
Which canonical state the counts were read from (FR-R5) — the identical string `knowledge.search` publishes as `retrieval.snapshotId`, so a caller holding one can compare it against the other without a second call and tell whether a search answered from the state this report describes.

Read from the same resolution of `.theurian/state/active.json` that chose the database these counts came from, not from a second read of the pointer. The two disagree exactly when `migrate apply` lands mid-request, and a hash naming a state the counts did not come from is worse than no hash at all.

**It moves for any change to canonical state, including a migration that creates only withheld items**, because it content-addresses the whole working tree by design (ADR-0016, ADR-0007): every migration file, every body file it references, and the schema and engine versions. It carries no bit about *what* changed — not a status, not an id, not a body — and it is query-independent by construction, which is the identical argument `snapshotId` carries and the reason FR-R5 publishes it at all. Removing it would remove the freshness contract this tool exists to serve. Accepted with that reasoning and the measurement in the top-level description ([#19](https://github.com/theurian/theurian/issues/19)).

itemCount.description:
The sum of `itemsByStatus`'s values, and deliberately not the number of items in the store.

Reporting the true total beside a filtered breakdown would hand back the withheld count exactly, by subtraction. A single aggregate withheld total was considered and rejected for the same reason a per-status one was: a caller who retires an item and watches one number move immediately afterwards has confirmed it, which is the oracle T-17 exists to close, only coarser.

So `0` here means "nothing you may see", not "nothing exists", and this number does not distinguish them — on purpose.

itemsByStatus.description:
How many items hold each status a caller may see. A key appears only when at least one item holds that status — a status with no items is absent rather than present with a zero — so `{}` is a valid and expected response.

**The three keys are exactly the surfaceable statuses** (`SURFACEABLE_STATUSES` in `theurian.domain.enums`), and `deprecated`, `superseded` and `rejected` can never appear. `additionalProperties: false` is what makes that a contract rather than a comment: a fourth key fails validation whatever it is named, so a breakdown that reported retired items under `other`, or under a relabelled bucket, is rejected too — it would leak the same quantity.

This tool takes no `includeUnapproved` flag, so the set is fixed rather than widened per caller. `draft` and `proposed` are counted here while `knowledge.search` withholds them by default: a count of work in progress is what a status report is for, and neither status is what SEC-13 withholds — retired knowledge is, and a rejected revision is where the secret that caused the rejection still lives.

approved.description: Items a team has agreed on. The only status default retrieval returns.

draft.description: Work in progress. Reachable through `knowledge.search` only with `includeUnapproved`.

proposed.description: Put forward and not yet decided. Reachable on the same terms as `draft`.

appliedMigrations.description:
How many migration files this project has applied — in a healthy project, one per row of the canonical store's migration history. It is how a caller confirms that `theurian migrate apply` landed, which is the question this tool was added to answer.

Read from the active pointer's own `migrationCount`, carried from the same resolution of `active.json` that chose the database, not counted back from the store's rows. The two are equal by construction on a healthy project — the state database is immutable once built — and diverge only under damage, where the pointer's count is the authoritative one and the disagreement, in either direction, is disclosed through `integrity` (#30) rather than published here as a silently smaller number. Reporting the live count instead was the silent under-report #30 exists to close: a corrupt `migration_history.project_id` dropped every row out of the `WHERE`, so the field answered `0` against a project that had applied several.

`minimum: 0` is enforced before the value is published, not merely declared here. The pointer is a file on disk and a hand-edited `migrationCount: -5` used to reach the wire verbatim; it is now refused at parse time with the remedy that rebuilds the pointer, because a response carrying it fails a strict client's validation *as a whole* — taking the `integrity` key that says the state is damaged down with it.

A count of *files*, never of items. It moves identically whether a migration created an approved item, a draft, a rejected one, or no item at all, so it cannot be made to name a status, an id, or a body. No request parameter reaches it: `knowledge.status` takes only `projectId`, so there is no probe to vary and therefore no extraction oracle — the same property that made `snapshotId` safe to publish and a per-query count of withheld matches unsafe.

**It does move when a migration creating only withheld items lands**, which `stateHash` already does for the same input. The one bit it adds over the hash is direction — a migration was added rather than an existing one edited — which is strictly coarser than what `stateHash` already distinguishes, and `stateHash` is staying: no bit reaches a caller here that the retained hash does not carry too. That direction is a property of the project's own migration directory, not of any caller's authorization to read that project — the daemon runs no per-caller access control (T-11). Accepted on those terms rather than removed, bucketed, or recomputed over surfaceable items only: the first two break the use the field exists for, and the third would publish a number no user can reproduce from their own migration files ([#19](https://github.com/theurian/theurian/issues/19)).

integrity.description:
Present **only** when a bounded integrity check detected a discrepancy: the derived state database holds a different number of `migration_history` rows for this project — fewer, or more — than the active pointer that chose that database records in its `migrationCount` (#30). That comparison is the whole of what this key measures, and the pointer's side of it is the number published above as `appliedMigrations`. The state database is immutable once built, so the two agree on a healthy project and any difference is damage: fewer when a row is lost or falls out of a `WHERE` — a sentinel in `migration_history.project_id` is what made this tool report `appliedMigrations: 0` against a project that had applied several, no value converted and nothing else in the response saying so — more when another project's rows reach this one. Hence a difference, not a shortfall.

**What it covers is the applied-migration count, not the item counts.** `itemCount` and `itemsByStatus` are read from `knowledge_items`, and a sentinel in `knowledge_items.project_id` or `knowledge_items.status` under-reports them while the migration rows stay intact: this tool answers `itemCount: 0` with *this key absent*, indistinguishable from a project that genuinely holds nothing. Those positions are the `SILENTLY_EMPTIED` members carried to PR2 (#30).

**Absence asserts nothing.** No `integrity` key means the check did not fire, which is *not* a clean bill of health and must not be read as one. The check is incomplete by design — this release (PR1) detects only a migration-count mismatch — so damage it does not yet cover leaves this key absent exactly as a healthy project does. There is deliberately no `damageDetected: false` form: a `false` token would read as "checked and clean" over an admittedly incomplete detector, louder than any description here, while absence, asserting nothing, cannot be misread without a caller inventing a claim. This is the same present-only contract `retrieval.snapshotId`'s sibling `raptorPath` already follows on the search side (ADR-0008 decision 8): the wire already branches on key presence.

Declared so `additionalProperties: false` continues to hold when the key is present.

damageDetected.description: Always `true` when this key is present — the object exists to report detected damage, so the field is redundant with presence by design. Kept explicit rather than reduced to a bare boolean so the signal can grow a second field (a code, a bound) without a wire break, and never carries `false`: there is no clean form of this object, only its absence.

remedy.description:
How to rebuild the derived state from the Git-tracked migrations. **Two steps, because one does not cure every shape this signal fires on.** `theurian migrate apply` comes first and is the cheap cure: a *lost* migration row is re-applied and the signal clears. A *surplus* row is not — the migration set is already fully applied, so that command exits 0 having changed nothing and the signal stays, measured over three consecutive runs. Deleting `.theurian/state/` is the universal cure and the one the state-refusal messages already print: the whole directory is derived (ADR-0004), so the next apply rebuilds the database from the migrations with exactly the recorded count.

That deletion takes a published retrieval index with it — measured, `retrieval.indexed` reads `false` afterwards until a rebuild — so the string names `theurian index build` too rather than curing this signal by silently downgrading the project to unranked scans.

One string, identical on every signal from every tool, and it never quotes the damaged cell.

schemaVersion.description:
The canonical store's SQLite schema version. Not the wire `protocolVersion`, and not the retrieval index's schema version — three different numbers, and this is the one that says how the knowledge database itself is laid out.

The version this daemon supports, which is also the version the database it just read holds: opening a store whose recorded version differs raises rather than reinterpreting the rows, so a response carrying this value is a response read from a store that matched it.

An input to `stateHash` (ADR-0017), so bumping it invalidates cached state instead of silently reinterpreting it — which is why two projects with identical knowledge and different schema versions do not share a hash.
